summary: Defines the CAA DNS resource record, which lets a domain holder list the Certification Authorities allowed to issue certificates for that domain. CAs check it before issuing, reducing the risk of mis-issued certificates. It was replaced by RFC 8659.

eli5.summary: You pin a note on your door saying only these locksmiths may make keys for it. A locksmith must read the note before making a key.

how to restrict which ca can issue certificates for my domain

subtitle: DNS records that list which certification authorities may issue certificates for a domain

tldr.problem: Certificate Authorities (CAs) can be tricked into issuing certificates for domains they should not issue for, leading to security breaches and mis-issued certificates.
tldr.mechanism: CAA DNS resource records allow domain holders to publish which CAs are authorized to issue certificates for their domain, and CAs check these records before issuing.
tldr.outcome: CAA records reduce the risk of certificate mis-issue by enabling CAs to verify authorization before issuing, though they do not prevent all attacks. This RFC was updated by RFC 8659.

today: RFC 6844 was superseded by RFC 8659 in September 2020, which made technical corrections and clarifications. CAA records are now a standard part of PKI infrastructure, widely deployed, and checked by most public CAs before issuing certificates.

sections.title: What CAA Records Do
sections.content:
The Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) DNS Resource Record lets a domain holder specify which Certificate Authorities (CAs) are authorized to issue certificates for that domain. When a CA receives a request to issue a certificate, it can check for a CAA record and see if it is on the list of authorized issuers.

Unlike DANE (which uses DNS to verify certificates after they are issued), CAA records are checked by the issuer before issuing the certificate. This allows CAs to implement additional controls and reduce the risk of mis-issued certificates.
sections.eli5: CAA is a DNS record that tells which locksmiths are allowed to make keys for your domain. A good locksmith checks the record before making a key.

sections.title: The CAA Record Format
sections.content:
A CAA resource record consists of a flags byte and a property tag-value pair. Multiple CAA records may exist for the same domain. The flags byte contains an Issuer Critical flag: if set to 1, the property tag must be understood by the issuer for the record to be correctly interpreted. Issuers MUST NOT issue certificates if a CAA record set contains unknown critical property tags.

The property tag is a short ASCII string (1 to 15 characters typically) such as issue, issuewild, or iodef. The property value varies depending on the tag. Values are encoded as binary data and may employ sub-formats.
sections.eli5: A CAA record has a flag (important or not) and a tag-value pair. The tag says what kind of permission it is, and the value says the details.

sections.title: CAA Properties
sections.content:
Three property tags are defined in this RFC:

issue authorizes a CA (specified by domain name) or parties acting under its authority to issue certificates for the domain. For example, CAA 0 issue "ca.example.net" authorizes only the CA at example.net to issue certificates.

issuewild has the same syntax and semantics as issue but only authorizes wildcard certificates (such as *.example.com). If issuewild properties are present, issue properties are ignored when processing wildcard requests.

iodef specifies a URL (via mailto, http, or https) to which an issuer may report certificate requests that are inconsistent with the issuer's policies or that violate the domain holder's stated policy.
sections.eli5: CAA has three types of rules: who can issue regular certificates, who can issue wildcard certificates, and where to report suspicious requests.

sections.title: How CAs Use CAA Records
sections.content:
Before issuing a certificate, a compliant CA MUST check for a relevant CAA resource record set. If one exists, the CA MUST NOT issue a certificate unless the request is consistent with the CAA records or an exception in the CA's Certificate Policy applies.

The CA searches the DNS name tree from the requested label upward (but not including the root). For example, when issuing for x.y.z, the CA searches x.y.z, then y.z, then z. CNAME and DNAME aliases are followed. The search stops when a CAA record set is found or the root is reached.

A domain holder may specify additional parameters as name-value pairs (for example, issue "ca.example.net; account=230123"). The semantics of these parameters are left to site policy and the CA.
sections.eli5: When someone asks a locksmith to make a key, the locksmith looks for a CAA record by checking the domain name and its parent domains. If the locksmith finds the CAA record and sees it is authorized, the locksmith can make the key.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
CAA records reduce the risk of certificate mis-issue but do not eliminate it. A CAA record is a necessary but not sufficient condition for issuing a certificate; the CA must still validate the certificate request according to its own Certificate Policy.

CAs should use DNSSEC to authenticate CAA records. Without DNSSEC, an attacker could suppress CAA records or insert bogus ones. However, even without DNSSEC, an issuer MUST NOT issue a certificate that conflicts with the relevant CAA record set.

Conformance with CAA records is checked at certificate issue time, not at validation time. A certificate that is not conformant with current CAA records may have been conformant when it was issued.
sections.eli5: CAA records help but are not perfect. A dishonest locksmith could ignore the note on the door. CAs should use DNSSEC to make sure the CAA record is real and not forged.

sections.title: Status
sections.content: CAA records were introduced in RFC 6844 as an Internet Standard. This RFC was later updated by RFC 8659, which made improvements to the specification. CAA records are now widely deployed and checked by most Certificate Authorities before issuing SSL/TLS certificates.
sections.eli5: CAA records are now used by real certificate authorities to protect domain owners from mis-issued certificates.
